title: Messaging in Spring: Kafka and RabbitMQ listeners, dead letters, outbox and idempotence
seriesDescription: Kafka and RabbitMQ with Spring, retries, circuit breakers and timeouts. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Spring for Apache Kafka and Spring AMQP: listeners, ack modes, error handlers and dead-letter topics, non-blocking retries, producer settings, and a transactional outbox with idempotent consumers.
source: Spring for Apache Kafka reference (listener containers, error handling, retryable topics); Spring AMQP reference; Spring Boot reference (spring.kafka.* properties); Apache Kafka producer and consumer configs; microservices.io transactional outbox

questions.prompt: Write a Spring for Apache Kafka listener method onOrder(String payload) that consumes the topic "orders" as consumer group "billing".
questions.model:
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "billing")
public void onOrder(String payload) { process(payload); }
questions.explanation: The RabbitMQ equivalent is @RabbitListener(queues = "orders"). With Kafka the group id decides who shares the partitions; two groups each receive every record.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring AMQP listener method onOrder(String body) that consumes messages from the RabbitMQ queue "orders".
questions.explanation: The queue must exist (declare a Queue bean or create it on the broker). Unlike Kafka there is no group id: competing consumers on one queue share its messages.

questions.prompt: A @RabbitListener throws an IllegalStateException for a message that can never be processed. Spring AMQP and its Boot auto-configuration are on defaults. What happens to the message?

options.text: It is dead-lettered after the third failure, because Boot enables stateless retries by default.
options.why: Stateless retry is not on by default, and no DLX exists unless you configure one.

options.text: It is acknowledged and dropped silently by the container so that the queue can keep moving.
options.why: Dropping needs an explicit non-requeue rejection; the default is to requeue.

options.text: It is rejected and requeued, then redelivered again and again.
options.why: Correct: defaultRequeueRejected is true, so a business exception requeues the message.

options.text: The listener container stops permanently and stays stopped until the application is restarted.
options.why: The container keeps running and keeps receiving the same message.

questions.explanation: Break the loop by throwing AmqpRejectAndDontRequeueException, setting spring.rabbitmq.listener.simple.default-requeue-rejected=false, or enabling listener retry with a recoverer. Add a dead-letter exchange so rejected messages are kept. Conversion failures are treated as fatal and are not requeued.

questions.prompt: Write a @KafkaListener method onPayment(String payload, Acknowledgment ack) for topic "payments" that processes the payload and then acknowledges the record, assuming the container uses AckMode.MANUAL.
questions.explanation: Acknowledging after processing gives at-least-once. Set spring.kafka.listener.ack-mode=manual (or manual_immediate) for the Acknowledgment argument to be supplied. If process throws, the error handler decides on retry or dead lettering and the offset is not committed.

questions.prompt: Match each Spring Kafka AckMode with when the offsets are committed.

right.text: After the listener has processed each individual record
After all records returned by one poll have been processed
After the listener calls acknowledge(), batched like BATCH
Immediately when the listener calls acknowledge()
Never: the broker assigns offsets automatically

questions.explanation: RECORD gives the most commits and the fewest duplicates after a crash; BATCH is the cheapest. MANUAL modes let you commit only after an external side effect succeeds.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring Kafka bean method errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) returning a DefaultErrorHandler that publishes failed records to a dead-letter topic with DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer and retries 3 times, 1 second apart, using a FixedBackOff.
questions.model:
return new DefaultErrorHandler(new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template), new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3));
}
questions.explanation: The recoverer publishes to <topic>.DLT by default. FixedBackOff(interval, maxAttempts) counts retries after the first delivery, so 3 means 4 deliveries in total. ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries is another valid way to add backoff, and DefaultErrorHandler treats some exceptions (such as deserialisation errors) as not retryable.

questions.prompt: A DefaultErrorHandler is configured with new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3). In the worst case, how many times is the listener invoked for one failing record before the record is recovered (sent to the dead-letter topic)?
questions.explanation: The first delivery plus 3 retries = 4 invocations. The second FixedBackOff argument is the maximum number of retries, not the total attempts.

questions.prompt: Add the annotation to a @KafkaListener method so that failures are retried through retry topics with 4 attempts in total and an exponential back-off starting at 1000 ms with multiplier 2.0, without blocking the main topic.
questions.explanation: Spring Kafka creates orders-retry-0, orders-retry-1 ... and a -dlt topic, so a slow retry never blocks other records on the main topic. The cost is that ordering across the retried record and later records is lost. attempts is a String in the annotation.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A record with an undeserialisable payload can keep a Spring Kafka consumer failing in a loop unless the value deserializer is wrapped in an ErrorHandlingDeserializer.
questions.reason: The poll() call throws while deserialising the bad record, before the listener or its error handler is ever invoked for it.

whys.a: Correct: Without the wrapper the failure happens inside the Kafka client, so the container cannot skip the record.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: ErrorHandlingDeserializer captures the failure and passes it to the container as a header, so DefaultErrorHandler can dead-letter it. Configure the delegate through spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A @Transactional @KafkaListener method makes the database write and the offset commit one atomic unit.
questions.reason: Offsets are stored in a Kafka topic, which is a separate system from the relational database.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: the JDBC transaction cannot include the Kafka offset commit unless Kafka transactions and chained transaction managers are set up. R is true.

questions.explanation: Without that setup you get at-least-once: a crash between the DB commit and the offset commit replays the record, so the write must be idempotent.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A RabbitMQ queue declared with x-dead-letter-exchange re-routes messages that a Spring AMQP listener rejects without requeue.
questions.reason: The dead-letter exchange feature only works for stream queues, not for classic or quorum queues.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true for classic and quorum queues. R is false.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Declare the DLX and dead-letter queue as beans (QueueBuilder.durable("orders").deadLetterExchange("orders.dlx")). The x-death header carries the reason and count.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Sending every event with the order id as the record key keeps the events of one order in order for its consumers.
questions.reason: Kafka stores consumer offsets in an internal topic called __consumer_offsets.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: Both are true, but the offsets topic has nothing to do with key-based ordering; the key-to-partition mapping does.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: KafkaTemplate.send("orders", orderId, payload) hashes the key to a partition, and one partition is read by one group member in order.

questions.prompt: True or false: calling kafkaTemplate.send(...) inside a @Transactional service method makes the Kafka publish roll back if the database transaction later rolls back.

options.why: KafkaTemplate sends through the Kafka client, which is not enlisted in a JDBC transaction by default.
Correct: the record may already be on the broker when the database rolls back, which is the dual-write problem.

questions.explanation: Use the transactional outbox: insert an event row in the same database transaction and publish it from a relay, or from log-based capture. Alternatively write an AFTER_COMMIT TransactionalEventListener, which still loses the event if the process dies after commit.

questions.prompt: Inside a @Transactional method placeOrder(Order o) that has OrderRepository orders and OutboxRepository outbox, write the two lines that save the order and save a new OutboxEvent("OrderCreated", o.getId()) so both commit atomically.

checks.label: does not publish to the broker

questions.explanation: Both rows commit or roll back together. A relay (a scheduled poller using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, or Debezium) publishes the outbox rows afterwards, giving at-least-once delivery.

questions.prompt: With a JdbcTemplate named jdbc and a String id, write the Java statement that inserts id into processed_messages(message_id) with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, storing the affected row count in an int named rows, then returns from the method when the message was already seen.

checks.label: returns when no row was inserted

questions.model:
int rows = jdbc.update("INSERT INTO processed_messages (message_id) VALUES (?) ON CONFLICT (message_id) DO NOTHING", id);
if (rows == 0) return;
questions.explanation: Run this in the same transaction as the business effect. The unique key turns an at-least-once delivery into effectively-once processing. Catching DuplicateKeyException is the alternative when you use a plain INSERT.

questions.prompt: A topic has 6 partitions. Two application instances run a @KafkaListener with concurrency = 4 in the same consumer group. How many container threads are actually assigned partitions across both instances?
questions.explanation: The two instances start 8 consumer threads, but 6 partitions can feed only 6 of them. The other 2 sit idle until a rebalance gives them work.

questions.prompt: Write the application.yml fragment that makes the Spring Boot Kafka producer wait for all in-sync replicas (acks all) and enables idempotence through the pass-through properties map.
questions.model:
spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
questions.explanation: Idempotence needs acks=all and keeps per-partition order with retries. Since Kafka 3.0 clients both are the default, but stating them makes the intent explicit and survives configuration overrides.

questions.prompt: Complete the Spring Boot Kafka consumer settings.
questions.text: Set spring.kafka.consumer.{1} to earliest so a new group replays retained history, keep the client setting {2} at false so offsets are committed by the listener container, and use isolation-level {3} to see only committed transactional records.
questions.explanation: The container commits according to its ack mode, so leaving client auto-commit on would add a second, uncoordinated commit path. auto-offset-reset only applies when the group has no valid committed offset.

questions.prompt: How can code using KafkaTemplate find out that a send(...) eventually failed after the client exhausted its retries?

options.text: Handle the CompletableFuture returned by send, or block on get().
options.why: Correct: the future completes exceptionally when delivery fails.

options.text: Wrap the send call in try/catch, because the failure is always thrown synchronously to the caller of send.
options.why: Delivery is asynchronous, so most failures arrive later via the future.

options.text: Check that the topic exists in the broker listing before every send and treat that as proof of delivery.
options.why: Topic existence says nothing about whether this record was delivered.

options.text: Read the consumer lag of the topic after a few seconds and compare it with the number of sends.
options.why: Lag measures consumers, not whether the producer succeeded.

questions.explanation: A fire-and-forget send silently loses failures. Also set delivery.timeout.ms and log or dead-letter from the callback. In Spring Kafka 3 the return type is CompletableFuture<SendResult>.
